items.item: The one-line derivation: a bit is still zero after kn settings with probability ≈ e^{-kn/m}; the false-positive rate (1 - e^{-kn/m})^k follows, "very close (within O(1/m))" to exact
The counting lower bound m ≥ n·log₂(1/ε), and Bloom's own optimum within a factor log₂e ≈ 1.44 of it

expert.by: self-review (no independent reviewer this session; see REVIEW.md)

items.item: Why setting an already-set bit again costs nothing and loses nothing: the structure only ever asks "is this bit one", never "who set this bit" or "how many times"
Why no false negative is ever possible by construction: a bit, once set, is never cleared, so every bit a real insert set stays set forever
Why the rate-vs-k curve has a flat valley near its minimum, and why that is exactly what licenses LevelDB's truncation and other implementations' rounding of k without a measurable cost

Why cutting the false-positive rate by ten thousand times costs a small, fixed number of extra bits per key rather than ten thousand times the memory: each extra bit per key multiplies the rate by a constant factor, so the cost of rarity is additive in bits, not multiplicative in space
Why the 1.44 gap between the Bloom filter's achievable rate and the information-theoretic floor is a fixed constant that never grows, no matter how rare the target rate gets

That the double-hashing arithmetic here (spreading k probes for one key) and Chapter 3's double hashing (resolving a collision between two keys) share the same formula shape but solve different problems, stated explicitly rather than left for the reader to notice

Why an immutable LSM run's filter never needs a delete at all: the run's key set is fixed at creation, and a logically deleted key is handled by a tombstone in a newer run, not by editing the old filter

The real implementation bug this topic's own build hit: a hand-rolled hash combiner can leave correlation between a key's k probes invisible to a glance at the code, inflating the real false-positive rate several times over the formula's prediction, caught only by measuring against the derived formula, not by reading the code

That the skipped structures (cuckoo, quotient, xor/binary-fuse/ribbon filters) exist specifically to beat one or both of this structure's two costs — no deletes, and the 1.44x gap — named once, not built, so a reader isn't left thinking the Bloom filter is the end of the story
